title: Introduce organic certification and internal control systems

lessons.title: What organic certification is
lessons.html:
Organic farming and the organic label

Organic farming produces food without synthetic fertilisers, synthetic pesticides, genetically modified seed or routine use of antibiotics and growth promoters. It builds soil health with compost, manure, crop rotation and cover crops, and manages pests with natural methods.

Buyers often pay more for organic products. But a buyer cannot see by looking at a carrot whether it was grown organically. That is why we need certification: an independent check that a farm follows an organic standard, so the product can be sold with an organic label.

The organic standard

A standard is a written set of rules. The standard used depends on the market: local buyers, South African retailers or export markets such as Europe may each require a particular standard. The standard covers things like:

  • Which inputs are allowed and which are not.
  • A conversion period before land can be sold as organic. The length is set by the standard.
  • Keeping organic and non-organic products apart.
  • Protecting fields from spray drift from neighbours, for example with buffer zones.
  • Animal welfare and feed for organic livestock.
  • Records that prove what was done.

How certification works

  1. The farm applies to a certification body.
  2. The farm completes forms describing fields, crops, inputs and practices.
  3. An inspector visits, walks the fields and stores and checks records.
  4. The certification body decides whether the farm complies.
  5. If it complies, a certificate is issued, usually valid for a year, with inspections repeated.

Small-scale farmers selling locally may also use a Participatory Guarantee System (PGS), where farmers and consumers check each other's farms. It costs less but is mostly accepted in local markets.

lessons.title: Internal control systems for farmer groups
lessons.html:
Why groups certify together

Certification costs money: application, inspection and fees. For a single smallholder with one or two hectares, this can be too expensive. Groups of small farmers, for example a co-operative of rooibos or vegetable growers, can be certified together using an Internal Control System (ICS).

What an ICS is

An ICS is the group's own system for making sure every member follows the organic standard. Instead of the outside inspector visiting every farm, the group inspects its own members. The certification body then checks that the ICS works well, and visits a sample of farms.

Parts of an ICS

PartWhat it means
ICS managerPerson who runs the system and keeps the files
Internal rulesThe organic standard explained in simple language for members
Member agreementsEach farmer signs that they will follow the rules
Farm registerList of members, field sizes, crops and expected harvest
Internal inspectorsTrained people who visit each farm at least yearly and fill in a report
Approval committeeDecides if each farmer complies, based on the reports
SanctionsAgreed actions when a farmer breaks the rules, such as a warning or removing the product from organic sales
TrainingRegular training of members and inspectors

Your role as a member or worker

  • Use only inputs allowed by the group rules. Ask the ICS manager if unsure.
  • Keep simple records: what you planted, which inputs you used, when you harvested and how much.
  • Keep organic produce separate in clean bags and crates, clearly marked.
  • Be honest with internal inspectors. One member's false claim can cost the whole group its certificate.
  • Report problems such as spray drift from a neighbour.

Key points

  • Certification is an independent check that a farm follows an organic standard.
  • Standards cover inputs, conversion, separation, buffer zones and records.
  • An inspector visits and a certification body decides on the certificate.
  • An ICS lets small farmer groups certify together by inspecting their own members.
  • Honest records and keeping organic produce separate protect the whole group.
